title: Authentication

definition.text: Authentication is the act of proving an assertion, such as the identity of a computer system user.

facts.text: Identification only indicates who a person or thing is; authentication is the process of verifying that identity.
In computing, a user's identity often has to be verified before access to confidential data or systems is allowed.
Authentication is distinct from authorization: authentication verifies that you are who you say you are, while authorization verifies that you are permitted to do what you are trying to do.
Authorization often follows authentication, but does not presuppose it: an anonymous agent could be authorized for a limited set of actions.
Credentials such as a password or key card imply authenticity without guaranteeing it.

Most secure internet communication relies on centralized trust, as in HTTPS where public certificate authorities vouch for the authenticity of websites; OpenID Connect rests on the same model, with identity providers such as Google authenticating users for other applications.
Decentralized peer-based trust, a web of trust as in PGP, has individuals personally verify and sign each other's cryptographic keys without a central authority.

notes: Other sections of the Wikipedia page (art, antiques, commercial products, literature) are about authenticating objects and are out of scope.

definition.text: Authentication factors are the three categories of evidence used to verify identity: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is.

facts.text: Each factor covers a range of elements used to verify a person's identity before granting access, approving a transaction, or signing a document.
Knowledge factors are things the user knows, such as a password, passphrase, PIN, challenge-response or security question.
Ownership factors are things the user has, such as an ID card, a security token, or a cell phone holding a software token.
Inherence factors are what the user is or does, such as a fingerprint, retinal pattern, face, voice, signature or other biometric identifier.
Security research has determined that a positive authentication should verify elements from at least two factors, and preferably all three.
Fingerprints were historically the most authoritative method, but court cases in the US and elsewhere have raised fundamental doubts about their reliability.

title: Multi-factor authentication

definition.text: Multi-factor authentication grants a user access only after they present two or more distinct types of evidence, or factors, to an authentication mechanism.

facts.text: MFA protects personal data from a third party who has discovered, for example, a single password, and accounts with MFA enabled are significantly less likely to be compromised.
The premise is that an unauthorized actor is unlikely to supply every required factor: if one is missing or wrong, the identity is not established and access stays blocked.
Two-factor authentication is the special case of exactly two factors, such as a bank card (something the user has) together with a PIN (something the user knows).
Several checks of one kind do not add up to more factors: fingerprints, a face and a PIN with a day code is still two-factor, and the FFIEC required distinct instances of the three factors.
Single-factor authentication, the weakest level, uses one component from one category, offers little protection from misuse, and is not recommended for financial or personally relevant transactions.

The European Central Bank defines strong authentication as a procedure based on two or more of the three authentication factors; it resembles multi-factor authentication with more rigorous requirements.

Physical security keys are generally the most secure MFA option and SMS the most commonly used; phone-based methods include push notifications, QR codes, one-time passwords and SMS, needing no extra token because users carry the phone.

PCI DSS requirement 8.3 requires MFA for remote access into a card data environment, and the second Payment Services Directive has required strong customer authentication on most electronic payments in the European Economic Area since 14 September 2019.

notes: Replaces the first-round entry, which rested on the Authentication page's subsection; now built on the Multi-factor authentication page. Business-network example, strong-authentication independence rule, physical-token and phone drawbacks are in mention_sent_ids.

title: Continuous authentication
article: Authentication#In computer science > Authentication types > Continuous authentication

definition.text: Continuous authentication keeps monitoring and verifying a user throughout a session, based on biometric traits, instead of only at the initial log-in.

facts.text: Conventional computer systems authenticate users only at the initial log-in, which can be a critical security flaw.
Systems resolve this by continuously monitoring and authenticating users based on biometric traits.
Smartphone sensors can extract behavioral attributes such as touch dynamics, keystroke dynamics and gait recognition to verify users implicitly and continuously.
Systems built on these behavioral biometric traits are known as active or continuous authentication systems.

title: Digital authentication
article: Authentication#In computer science > Authentication types > Digital authentication

definition.text: Digital authentication, also called electronic authentication, is a group of processes that establish and present confidence in user identities to an information system by electronic methods.

facts.text: It is technically challenging because individuals or entities must be authenticated remotely over a network.
In NIST's generic model, enrollment has an applicant prove their identity to a credential service provider (CSP), after which the applicant becomes a subscriber.

The subscriber then receives an authenticator such as a token plus credentials such as a user name, and proves possession of an authenticator in a session with a relying party; the CSP maintains the credential over its life cycle.
Electronic communication is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, where a third party poses as each of two parties; extra identity factors can be required to authenticate each party.

definition.text: A system stores each password as a hash of the password plus a unique random salt, never as plain text or a bare hash.

facts.text: Plain-text passwords are a bad idea because anyone with internal access can see them.
Storing bare password hashes is not enough because they are prone to precomputation attacks such as rainbow tables; salting the passwords mitigates this.
According to OWASP, a salt is a unique, randomly generated string added to each password as part of the hashing process.
A salt is not meant to be secret and can be stored in plain text in the database; it makes the hash result unique to each password.
The database stores the hash of the password plus the salt.
To validate a login, the system fetches the user's salt, appends it to the entered password, hashes it, and compares the result with the stored hash; if they match, the password is valid.

definition.text: A website manages a logged-in user's identity with sessions, tokens, JSON Web Tokens, single sign-on, OAuth 2.0 or QR-code login.

facts.text: With a session, the server stores the user's identity and gives the browser a session ID cookie, which lets the server track login state; cookies do not work well across devices.
With a token, the identity is encoded into a token the browser sends on later requests, so no server session storage is needed, but tokens need encryption and decryption.
JSON Web Tokens standardize identity tokens and use digital signatures for trust; the signature travels inside the token, so no server session is needed.
Single sign-on uses a central authentication service so that one login works across multiple sites.
OAuth 2.0 lets one site get limited access to your data on another site without being given your passwords.
QR-code login encodes a random token into a QR code, and scanning it logs the user in on mobile without typing a password.

title: OAuth 2.0

definition.text: OAuth 2.0 is an open standard for access delegation that lets a user grant an application consented access to resources on another site without sharing credentials.

facts.text: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, not an authentication protocol: it is designed primarily to grant access to a set of resources such as remote APIs or a user's data.

Four roles take part: the resource owner owns the protected resources, the client needs access to them, the authorization server issues access tokens after authentication and consent, and the resource server validates tokens and returns resources.
Scopes specify exactly why access may be granted; the acceptable scope values and the resources they relate to depend on the resource server.
An access token represents authorization to access resources on behalf of the end-user; an authorization server issues it to a third-party client with the resource owner's approval.
An app holding an OAuth token can reach only the parts of the user's profile that the user allowed.
OAuth 1 is specified in RFC 5849 and OAuth 2 in RFC 6749.
Singh lists three common disadvantages of OAuth 2.0: it lacks built-in security features, has no standard implementation, and has no common set of scopes.

Eran Hammer, a former lead author, argued that OAuth 2.0 became more complex, less interoperable and less secure than 1.0, because it removed protocol-level signatures and cryptography and left many items for implementations to decide.

notes: Wikipedia's History and Uses sections (people, companies and which sites support OAuth) are not drafted: they are business and product history.

definition.text: In the OAuth 2.0 flow a client obtains an access token from the authorization server, with the resource owner's consent, and uses it to request resources from the resource server.

facts.text: The client requests authorization from the authorization server, supplying its client id and secret as identification, the scopes it wants, and an endpoint URI to receive the access token or authorization code.
The authorization server authenticates the client and verifies that the requested scopes are permitted, and the resource owner interacts with it to grant access.
The authorization server redirects back to the client with an authorization code or an access token, depending on the grant type, and may also return a refresh token.
With the access token the client asks the resource server for the resource; the resource server accepts and validates the token and returns the appropriate resources.

An access token is provided through an authorization grant, also called an authorization flow, and the framework specifies several grant types for different use cases, such as Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC).

sources.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) (Singh's System Design)

definition.text: OpenID Connect is a thin authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds login and profile information about the person who is logged in.

facts.text: OAuth 2.0 only grants access to data and features from one application to another; OpenID Connect lets clients verify an end user's identity from the authorization server's authentication and fetch basic profile information.
It specifies a RESTful HTTP API with JSON as the data format, so web, mobile and JavaScript clients can request information about authenticated sessions and end users.
An authorization server that supports OIDC is sometimes called an Identity Provider, because it returns information about the resource owner to the client.
In OIDC the relying party is the current application, and the OpenID provider gives it a one-time code, which the token endpoint exchanges for an access code valid for an hour.

The main difference from plain OAuth 2.0 is that the token is provided as a JSON Web Token, and the relying party calls the UserInfo endpoint with a secure token to get information about the end user.
The OIDC specification is stricter than basic OAuth and is extensible, with optional features such as identity-data encryption, discovery of providers, and session management.
Because OIDC sits on top of OAuth, it has a built-in permission layer asking the user to agree to what the service provider may access; SAML achieves consent only by developer hard-coding.

sources.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) (Singh's System Design)

definition.text: Single sign-on is an authentication scheme in which a user logs in once, with a single set of credentials, to reach several related but independent applications.

facts.text: It removes the need to log in separately to each application, and true single sign-on lets the user access services without re-entering authentication factors.
Credentials and identity information are kept and managed by a central Identity Provider, a trusted system that gives access to other websites and applications.

In the flow, the user requests a resource, the application redirects them to the identity provider, the user signs in, the identity provider sends a single sign-on response to the application, and the application grants access.

Single sign-on differs from same sign-on, where every application still asks for authentication but reuses credentials from a directory server; true single sign-on passes one authentication token to the configured applications.

Because applications support different authentication mechanisms, single sign-on must store the credentials used at first sign-in and translate them for each system; the converse, single log-out, ends access to several systems with one action.

Schemes such as OpenID Connect can be configured for single sign-on if extras like user consent are disabled; federated social logons that ask for consent choices are not always single sign-on in the strictest sense.
Benefits include one set of credentials to remember, less password fatigue, enforced security and compliance, and lower IT support cost and administration time.

It is commonly used in enterprises where employees need many of the organization's applications; a simple version over IP networks uses cookies, but only if the sites share a common DNS parent domain.

definition.text: An identity provider is a centralized trusted system that stores and manages user identities and authenticates users on behalf of other applications.

facts.text: It authenticates a user either by validating a username and password or by validating an assertion about the user's identity from a separate identity provider.
It manages user identities so that service providers are freed from that responsibility; service providers rely on it to assert who a user is and typically to manage certain user attributes.
A service provider may still keep a local account for the user, holding attributes unique to its own service.
An identity broker is an intermediary connecting many service providers with different identity providers, so single sign-on works with any application regardless of the protocol it follows.

title: SAML
article: Single sign-on#Common configurations > Security Assertion Markup Language

definition.text: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an open XML-based standard for sharing identity, authentication and permission information between systems, such as an identity provider and a service provider.

facts.text: SAML enables identity federation: identity providers securely pass authenticated identities and their attributes to service providers.

In SAML single sign-on, the user requests a resource at a service provider, which sends an authentication request to the identity provider through the user's browser and trusts the identity information it gets back.

SAML passes XML messages and is geared to enterprise security, but it can be complex to install and maintain, while OAuth and OIDC use JSON and RESTful communication that suit mobile and modern web applications.
SAML sets a session cookie in the browser, which suits short-lived workloads.

title: Secure system design checklist

definition.text: Designing secure systems protects sensitive information and keeps the infrastructure stable and reliable, so developers should apply security guidelines by default.

facts.text: The guide's key design points are authentication, authorization, encryption, vulnerability, network security, terminal security, container security, API security, audit and compliance, emergency responses, third-party vendor management and disaster recovery.
Authentication: multiple factors work on the premise that an unauthorized actor is unlikely to supply them all, and WebAuthn verifies identity with digital signatures rather than shared passwords.
Passwords are stored as salted hashes: a unique salt per password defeats precomputed rainbow tables and keeps repeated passwords from showing up as identical hashes.
Authorization: the principle of least privilege gives accounts and processes only the privileges essential to their intended functions.

Vulnerability: XSS lets attackers inject scripts into pages other users view, countered by contextual output encoding, and CSRF is countered by embedding extra authentication data such as unique tokens in requests.
Network security: zero trust does not trust users and devices by default, even on a corporate LAN, and verifies identity and device compliance before granting least-privilege access.
Encryption in transit: OAuth forbids sending tokens or passwords in the clear and requires TLS with server authentication on its endpoints to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

notes: thin: the guide itself only names the design points; sentences from other pages now explain authentication, password storage, authorization, vulnerabilities, network security and encryption in transit, but nothing explains audit and compliance, emergency responses, third-party vendor management, disaster recovery, terminal security, container security or encryption at rest.

title: API security practices

facts.text: The guide's tips are: use OAuth2, use WebAuthn, use leveled API keys, authorization, rate limiting, whitelisting, an API gateway, error handling, input validation, API versioning, and check the OWASP API security risks.
With OAuth 2.0 an access token replaces the user's password with a single token the resource server understands, and can carry fewer rights than the grant that produced it.
Clients should request the minimal scope necessary, and the server may issue less than requested; tokens must be sent only over TLS, never in the clear.
WebAuthn grew from U2F, which improved on TOTP and SMS codes that stayed open to phishing, and it verifies the user's identity with digital signatures.
Authorization should follow least privilege: every module, user or program may access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

Input validation guards against code injection, where an unsanitized input modifies application logic; OAuth requires servers and clients to sanitize and validate any value received, in particular the state and redirect_uri parameters.
Rate limiting matters for credentials: without it an attacker can try an arbitrary number of codes until one works, and a limit tied to a session ID can be reset by creating new sessions.

notes: thin: the guide is a bare list of tips; sentences from other pages now explain OAuth2, WebAuthn, authorization, input validation and rate limiting, but nothing explains leveled API keys, whitelisting, API gateway use, error handling, API versioning or the OWASP API security risks.

title: Authorization

definition.text: Authorization is the function of specifying rights to access resources, usually through an access policy, and then deciding whether a particular subject may access a particular resource.

facts.text: Subjects can be human users, software or hardware; resources can be files, data, programs, devices or functionality provided by applications.

Authorization is closely related to access control, which enforces the policy by approving or rejecting access requests from authenticated consumers; it should not be confused with authentication, which verifies identity.
Identity and access management has two phases: a configuration phase that creates the user account and defines its access policy, and a usage phase where authentication is followed by access control.
By the principle of least privilege, consumers should be authorized to access only what they need to do their jobs, and nothing more.
Broken authorization is often listed as the number one risk in web applications.
On a distributed system it is often desirable to grant access without a unique identity; keys, certificates and tickets are access tokens that grant access without proving identity.

Maintaining authorization data is not trivial and often costs as much administration as managing authentication credentials; changing a user's authorization means changing or deleting the corresponding access rules.
Atomic authorization is an alternative to per-system management, in which a trusted third party securely distributes the authorization information.

notes: Wikipedia's related interpretations (public policy, banking, publishing) are other senses of the word and are not drafted.

title: Access control models

definition.text: Access control models are the ways an authorization policy is expressed and checked, such as access control lists, roles, attributes and relationships.

facts.text: Authorizations are expressed as access policies, for example as an access control list or a capability, or through a policy language such as XACML.
In role-based access control (RBAC), subjects are granted one or more roles, and access is allowed when the resource has been assigned at least one of those roles.
Relationship-based access control is gaining prominence with the rise of social media.

XACML is a policy-based, attribute-based framework that can weigh attributes of the user, action, resource and context; it supplies the policy language that OAuth lacks, while OAuth handles consent and access delegation.

notes: Role-based, attribute-based and relationship-based access control each have a Wikipedia page that is not crawled; see gaps.

definition.text: A JSON Web Token (JWT) is an Internet standard for creating data, optionally signed and optionally encrypted, whose JSON payload asserts a number of claims.

facts.text: JWT is a Proposed Standard, RFC 7519, and relies on the JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption standards.
Tokens are signed with a private secret or a public/private key pair; one party, usually the server, signs with its private key and anyone holding the matching public key can verify the token.
Tokens are compact and URL-safe, and their claims can pass the identity of authenticated users between an identity provider and a service provider.
A JWT has three parts: a header naming the signing algorithm, a payload containing a set of claims, and a signature that validates the token; each is Base64url-encoded and joined with periods.
The signature is computed over the encoded header and payload using the algorithm named in the header, typically HMAC with SHA-256 (HS256) or RSA signature with SHA-256 (RS256).

The specification defines seven registered claims, including issuer (iss), subject (sub), audience (aud), expiration time (exp), not before (nbf), issued at (iat) and JWT ID (jti); custom claims are usually added.
A token must not be accepted on or after its expiration time, and a principal that is not named in a present audience claim must reject the token.

The client sends the JWT in the Authorization header with the Bearer schema; the server checks it, and because user state is never kept in server memory and the token is self-contained, this is stateless and avoids repeated database queries.

A JWT's contents cannot be relied on in a trust decision unless they are cryptographically secured and bound to its context, and the signing key must verifiably be under the control of the party named as issuer.

Some JWT libraries validated tokens wrongly based on the alg field, most commonly by accepting alg=none; developers should never let the JWT header alone drive verification and should not depend on the alg field alone.
Even a token that validates should be rejected unless the algorithms it uses are acceptable to the application, because which algorithms may be used in a given context is an application decision.
A JWT should be sent to the client by a secure mechanism such as an HTTP-only cookie, because local or session storage can be read by client-side JavaScript, including browser extensions.

If a service must be able to invalidate a session before the token expires, it can no longer trust the token alone and must check a data store, which removes the statelessness that is the main advantage of JWTs.

A JWT may carry privacy-sensitive information. Prevent disclosure by encrypting the token and authenticating the recipient, or by sending it only over an encrypted protocol with endpoint authentication such as TLS; omitting the data is simplest.
Some have argued that JWTs are hard to use securely because the standard offers many algorithms and options, and that alternate standards should be used instead.

title: OAuth pseudo-authentication
article: OAuth#OAuth and other standards > OpenID vis-à-vis pseudo-authentication using OAuth

definition.text: Pseudo-authentication means using OAuth on its own as a login method, even though OAuth is an authorization protocol that says nothing about who the user is.

facts.text: OAuth tells the application nothing about the user or whether they are present: the client asked for a token, got one, and used it, without knowing who authorized it or whether a user was there at all.
Much of the point of OAuth is delegated access where the user is not present, which suits client authorization but is bad for authentication, where the point is to find out who is there.
In OpenID authentication the identity provider's response is an assertion of identity; in the OAuth case it is an access token, a kind of valet key giving ongoing access to some of its APIs.

Because the identity provider usually authenticates the user while granting a token, treating a successful token request as authentication is tempting, but OAuth was not designed for it and the assumption can cause major security flaws.

A stolen valet key lets an attacker impersonate its user to any application relying on OAuth2 for pseudo-authentication against the same authorization server; OpenID's cryptographic verification prevents this.
OpenID lets a user use one set of credentials across many sites, while OAuth lets one site access and use information about the user's account on another.
OpenID Connect fixes this by being an authentication layer built on top of OAuth 2.0.

title: OAuth 2.0 security threats

facts.text: An attacker who alters redirect_uri can have the authorization code sent to a URI they control; the server must check the URI used to get the code matches the one used to redeem it, and public clients must register theirs.

An open redirector forwards a user-agent to a parameter-given location without validation; if clients may register only part of a redirection URI, an attacker can use one to capture the code or token (RFC 6819's Open Redirector, later Covert Redirect).

CSRF against a client's redirection URI lets an attacker inject their own code or token; the client must bind requests to the user-agent's state with a non-guessable state parameter, and the authorization endpoint needs CSRF protection too.

In clickjacking an attacker loads the authorization page in a transparent iframe over dummy buttons; native apps should use external browsers, and servers can send an x-frame-options header of deny or sameorigin.

In the implicit flow the token travels in the URI fragment and an attacker can swap a stolen token into the response; delegated sign-in must not use implicit without extra measures such as audience-restricting the token.

Access tokens, refresh tokens, passwords and client credentials must not be sent in the clear; the server must require TLS on its endpoints and the client must validate its certificate, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

Formal analysis found that with several authorization servers, one malicious, a client can be confused about which to use and forward secrets to the malicious one (the AS Mix-Up Attack); a security best-current-practice draft followed.
The PKCE extension (RFC 7636) is recommended for all types of OAuth client in the draft of OAuth 2.1, and OpenID Connect mandates strict measures that preclude open redirectors.

notes: Replaces the first-round entry: RFC 6749 section 10 (standard tier) now carries the threats, the four old Wikipedia facts are re-cited. The 2017 phishing campaign that abused OAuth consent is a security incident and is not drafted.

title: OpenID

definition.text: OpenID is an open, decentralized authentication protocol that lets users sign in to many sites through a third-party identity provider.

facts.text: A site, called the relying party, authenticates users through a third-party identity provider, so the site needs no ad hoc login system and users need no separate identity and password for each site.
The identity provider gives the user a unique identifier, an OpenID; on a supporting site the user is redirected to their identity provider, which prompts them to authenticate.

A user can use a URL they control, such as a blog, as a delegated identity, and the Attribute Exchange extension lets the identity provider pass attributes such as name and gender to the relying party.
A malicious relying party can send users to a bogus identity provider page to steal credentials, and the identity provider keeps a log of every OpenID login, which makes cross-site tracking easier.

notes: OpenID Connect is the third generation of OpenID technology (c058de6c4356) and has its own entry. History, adoption figures, the OpenID Foundation and legal sections are not drafted.

title: Single sign-on risks

facts.text: Because one login unlocks many resources, stolen credentials do more damage and a compromised main SSO password exposes every supported application; SSO should ideally be paired with strong methods such as smart cards and one-time password tokens.
Single sign-on increases dependence on highly available authentication systems: losing them can deny access to every system unified under it, although session failover can keep operation going.
Where access must be guaranteed at all times, such as security or plant-floor systems, the risk of failure may make single sign-on undesirable.

Authentication is slower than traditional authentication because every application must ask the SSO provider to verify; some call it reduced sign-on, since different security levels may need more than one authentication server.

The SSO token cannot be protected with the HttpOnly cookie flag, so an XSS flaw on the logged-out website can let an attacker steal it and hijack the session; a stolen SSO session reaches every site using the SSO system.

Kerberos and SAML single sign-on originally gave users no choice about releasing personal information to each resource; as federated services spread and privacy rules such as the GDPR tighten, OpenID Connect has become more attractive.

notes: The 2012 social-login research findings and the 2020 breach mentioned on the Wikipedia page are incidents and are not drafted.

title: Single sign-on configurations

facts.text: In Kerberos-based single sign-on, the initial sign-on gets a ticket-granting ticket, which other applications such as email clients, wikis and revision-control systems use to acquire service tickets proving the user's identity without another prompt.
In smart-card-based single sign-on, the initial sign-on prompts for the smart card, which other applications then use too, with either certificates or passwords stored on the card.

Integrated Windows Authentication is Microsoft's term for SPNEGO, Kerberos and NTLMSSP authentication, most often the automatic authentication between its web server and browser; vendors extended it to Unix and Linux.

Mobile devices can log users onto many systems, such as building-access and computer systems, using OpenID Connect or SAML with an X.509 certificate identifying the device, which counts as something you have.

notes: Article is the first of several Common configurations subsections of Single sign-on (Kerberos, smart card, Integrated Windows Authentication, mobile); the SAML subsection is its own entry.

definition.text: MFA can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws.

facts.text: Many MFA approaches remain vulnerable to phishing, man-in-the-browser and man-in-the-middle attacks, so users should not share verification codes with anyone.

SMS codes are weak: phones can be cloned, maintenance personnel can read texts, SS7 vulnerabilities let messages be redirected to attackers, and SIM swap attacks hand duplicate SIM cards to criminals.

An MFA fatigue attack floods a user with push login requests until one is accepted by mistake; number matching is an interim mitigation, and phishing-resistant MFA is advised instead of push notifications.

Implementation flaws bypass MFA too: tokens issued before MFA must not reach sensitive resources, and without rate limiting an attacker can guess codes, resetting a limit tied to a session ID with new sessions.

definition.text: A salt is random data fed as an additional input to a one-way function that hashes a password or passphrase.

facts.text: The salt and the password are concatenated and hashed, and the output hash is stored with the salt; the salt needs no encryption because knowing it would not help the attacker.
Without a salt, identical passwords map to identical hashes; a fresh salt per password gives different hashes for the same password, so reading the hashes does not reveal that two accounts share one.

Salting defeats partially precomputed tables such as rainbow tables by vastly growing the table needed, since it would have to cover salt plus hash; building tables for every unique salt is not viable.
With unique salts an attacker must hash each guess separately against every entry, so a single attempt cannot crack multiple passwords.
A unique salt is generated for each password, usually with a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator.
A salt of 16 bytes (128 bits) or more is generally sufficient; a short salt lets an attacker precompute a table of every possible salt appended to every likely password.
Reusing one salt for all passwords is dangerous: a precomputed table that accounts for the salt becomes viable, and cracking one hash also exposes others with the same password.
Without a salt a successful SQL injection attack may yield easily crackable passwords, and because many users re-use passwords across sites, salting is an important part of web application security.

definition.text: A rainbow table is a precomputed table of cryptographic hash outputs, usually used to recover passwords from stolen hashes.

facts.text: Rainbow tables trade space for time: less processing time and more storage than brute force, but more processing time and less storage than a table holding the hash of every possible password.
They store only the start and end of long chains built by alternating the hash function with reduction functions, using a different reduction function per column so colliding chains do not merge.
A table is specific to one hash function, such as MD5, and is ineffective against hashes with large salts, because the attacker would need a table for each possible salt value.

Key stretching, running salt, password and intermediate hashes through the hash function many times, also slows precomputation; rainbow tables saw reduced use as of 2020 as salting spread and GPU brute force became practical.

title: bcrypt

definition.text: bcrypt is a password-hashing function, based on the Blowfish cipher, designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières.

facts.text: It incorporates a salt against rainbow table attacks and is adaptive: the iteration count can be raised over time, so it stays resistant to brute-force search as computing power grows.
Its expensive key setup uses both salt and password and repeats a configurable number of rekeying rounds, so the hashing can be made arbitrarily slow, which deters brute force.
Inputs are a password of up to 72 bytes, a cost and a 16-byte salt; the cost is log2 of the iterations, so 12 means 4,096; the output is a 24-byte hash.
Passwords are cut at 72 bytes, only 18 characters in the worst case of 4-byte UTF-8, and bcrypt is not a key derivation function: it cannot derive a 512-bit key from a password.

notes: The article argues bcrypt beats Argon2 for run times under about one second and Argon2 wins only with high parameters; that opinion is kept out of the facts (sent_ids 1c1b4d22ca00, f7ba11b54c90, 493d4eba354a in mention_sent_ids).

definition.text: Argon2 is a key derivation function that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition.

facts.text: It uses a large, fixed-size memory region to make brute-force attacks computationally expensive, and all three modes are tuned by execution time, memory required and degree of parallelism.

Argon2d maximizes resistance to GPU cracking with password-dependent memory access, which risks side-channel attacks; Argon2i accesses memory independently of the password to resist them; Argon2id is a hybrid of the two.
RFC 9106 recommends Argon2id if one does not know the difference between the types or if side-channel attacks are a viable threat, partly because published attacks target Argon2i.
RFC 9106 recommends 2 GiB of memory, 1 iteration and parallelism 4 as a default for all environments, and 64 MiB, 3 iterations and parallelism 4 for memory-constrained environments.

definition.text: WebAuthn is a W3C web standard defining an API that websites use to authenticate users with public-key credentials, commonly called passkeys.

facts.text: It verifies identity with digital signatures instead of shared passwords, avoiding password flaws such as reuse across services, weak choices and improper server-side storage.
An authenticator, a device or program, proves to the website through the browser that the user possesses it; the standard defines a registration ceremony and an authentication ceremony.

The authenticator uses public-key cryptography to sign an assertion for the website; at registration its signed attestation statement carries the public key the website later uses to verify those assertions.

Platform authenticators are built into the operating system, such as Windows Hello and Apple Keychain; roaming ones connect over USB, Bluetooth Low Energy or NFC using CTAP; password managers can also serve.

The Web Authentication API extends the Credential Management API's navigator.credentials.create() and get() to accept a publicKey parameter: create() registers an authenticator and get() authenticates.

It resists some phishing because the authenticator only offers credentials registered on the same website, can run passwordless, and a roaming hardware authenticator resists malware as its keys sit on a separate device.

WebAuthn grew from U2F, which improved on TOTP and SMS codes that left users open to phishing; although touted as a password replacement, most sites implementing it still use passwords in some capacity.

definition.text: Kerberos is a ticket-based network authentication protocol that lets nodes on a non-secure network prove their identity to one another securely.

facts.text: It targets the client-server model and gives mutual authentication, with both user and server verifying each other, and its messages are protected against eavesdropping and replay attacks.
It builds on symmetric-key cryptography and needs a trusted third party, the key distribution center (KDC), whose authentication server (AS) and ticket-granting service (TGS) issue the tickets.

At logon the client authenticates to the AS, which returns a time-stamped ticket-granting ticket (TGT) encrypted with the TGS's secret key; the password is never sent, and v5 clients prove knowledge with an encrypted timestamp.
To use a service the client sends the TGT to the TGS, which checks it and issues a service ticket and session keys; the client presents the ticket to the service server with its request.
The service decrypts the ticket with its own secret key and checks the client's authenticator; it answers with the timestamp encrypted under the session key, so the client can trust the server.
Tickets have a lifetime, so hosts' clocks must be synchronized within configured limits (five minutes apart by default in MIT's setup) or authentication fails; NTP daemons usually keep them in sync.
Because a central KDC controls all authentications, compromising it lets an attacker impersonate any user, and each network service with a different host name needs its own Kerberos keys.
Windows 2000 and later use Kerberos as the default method for domain-joined clients, and fall back to NTLM when client or server is not part of the same trusted domain environment.

definition.text: The principle of least privilege requires that every module, such as a process, user or program, be able to access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

facts.text: Accounts and processes get only the privileges essential to their intended functions: an account that only creates backups may run backup applications and cannot install software.
Limiting code's system-wide actions means a vulnerability in one application cannot be used to exploit the rest of the machine, protecting data and functionality from faults and malicious behavior.
Code with limited scope is easier to test for its possible actions and interactions, and the fewer privileges an application requires, the easier it is to deploy.
Jerome Saltzer's original formulation: every program and every privileged user of the system should operate using the least amount of privilege necessary to complete the job.

Least privilege is associated with privilege bracketing, assuming privileges at the last possible moment and dismissing them as soon as unnecessary; giving a user read/write access to a file violates it if read suffices.

True least privilege is hard: practice removes privileges judged unnecessary, leaving more than the true minimum, and operating environments rarely control a process's access to memory, time or I/O precisely enough.

definition.text: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a web-application vulnerability that lets attackers inject client-side scripts into pages viewed by other users.

facts.text: An XSS flaw can bypass access controls such as the same-origin policy, and its effects range from a petty nuisance to a significant security risk depending on the sensitivity of the data the site handles.

The same-origin policy gives content from URLs with the same scheme, host name and port the same permissions; injected script arrives from the trusted site, so it runs with that site's permissions and can reach session cookies.
XSS is a case of code injection; in the 2021 and 2025 editions of the OWASP Top 10 it is grouped under the Injection category.

Reflected (non-persistent) XSS arises when client data, usually query parameters, is used immediately by server-side scripts to build a page without sanitizing, as when a search page echoes the query, and is delivered by a crafted link.
Stored (persistent) XSS is more devastating: the server saves the attacker's data and displays it to other users on normal pages, as on a message board that lets users post HTML.
In DOM-based XSS the malicious data never touches the web server; client-side JavaScript reflects it into the page, a class that arose as applications moved presentation logic into the browser.
Mutated XSS injects markup that looks safe but is rewritten by the browser while parsing, making it extremely hard to detect or sanitize; self-XSS instead tricks the victim into running the code.

title: XSS prevention
article: Cross-site scripting#Preventive measures > Contextual output encoding/escaping of string input

facts.text: Contextual output encoding escapes untrusted strings for where they land in the document (HTML entity, JavaScript, CSS or URL escaping); apps that need no rich input can largely eliminate XSS this way, and some template systems pick the encoder.

When users may submit HTML, output encoding is not enough because the browser must render it; untrusted HTML needs a sanitization engine that lets safe elements through and escapes dangerous ones such as script tags.

Session cookies are a target because client-side scripts can read them; an HttpOnly flag makes a cookie unavailable to scripts and SameSite=Strict strips it from cross-origin requests, though neither fully prevents XSS.

Trusted Types make web APIs check that values are marked trusted, so an attacker controlling a JavaScript string cannot cause XSS; DOM-based XSS needs input validation and escaping implemented in the page's JavaScript.

definition.text: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is an exploit in which a web application receives unauthorized commands from a user that it trusts.

facts.text: An innocent user is tricked into submitting a web request they did not intend; image tags, hidden forms or JavaScript requests can send it without their knowledge, changing session state or the user's account.
Unlike XSS, which exploits the trust a user has in a site, CSRF exploits the trust a site has in a user's browser.
Browsers automatically and invisibly include a domain's cookies, session cookies among them, in any request to that domain, so a forged request from another page looks genuine to the server.

An attack needs a site without CSRF protection, a state-changing action, input values the attacker can determine, and a victim logged in; data-only requests are useless because the attacker never sees the response.
GET is meant to be safe and not change state, yet a GET can be forged with an IMG tag; applications using GET for state-changing operations should switch to POST or add anti-CSRF protection.
Login CSRF forges a request that logs the victim into the target site with the attacker's credentials, so the attacker can later log in and view private activity history saved in that account.
Most CSRF defenses embed additional authentication data in requests so the application can detect requests coming from unauthorized locations.
The synchronizer token pattern embeds a secret, unique token in every HTML form and verifies it on the server, so the attacker cannot put a correct token in forged requests.

In the cookie-to-header technique, the server sets a random token cookie, client-side JavaScript copies it into a custom HTTP header on each transactional request, and the server validates the token's presence and integrity.

A double submit cookie sets the token as a cookie and also as a hidden form field and checks they match; the server stores no token, but the scheme can be bypassed if the site has cookie-setting functionality.
The SameSite cookie attribute set to strict makes the browser send the cookie only on same-site requests, making CSRF ineffective, though the browser must recognise and correctly implement it.

Checking the Origin or Referer header is another approach; a request omitting Referer must be treated as unauthorized because attackers can suppress it, which can break browsers or proxies that omit it for privacy.

definition.text: Zero trust is a security strategy in which users and devices are not trusted by default, even on a privileged network such as a corporate LAN or if previously verified.

facts.text: It is implemented by establishing identity verification, validating device compliance before granting access, and ensuring least privilege access to only explicitly authorized resources.
Trusting users and devices inside a corporate perimeter or behind a VPN is commonly not sufficient for networks of many zones, cloud services, remote and mobile environments and IoT devices.
Zero trust advocates mutual authentication that checks the identity and integrity of users and devices regardless of location, granting access by confidence in user identity and device status.
NIST SP 800-207 defines zero trust as concepts that reduce the uncertainty of enforcing accurate per-request access decisions when the network is viewed as compromised.
A full solution includes enhanced identity governance with policy-based access controls, micro-segmentation, and overlay networks or software-defined perimeters.
Applied to data, every request to access it is authenticated dynamically with least privilege, using attribute-based access control on attributes of the data, the user and the environment.

definition.text: An authorization grant is a credential representing the resource owner's authorization that the client uses to obtain an access token; RFC 6749 defines four grant types and a way to add more.

facts.text: In the authorization code grant the client sends the resource owner to the authorization server, which authenticates them and returns an authorization code, so the owner's credentials are never shared with the client.

The code lets the server authenticate the client and delivers the access token directly to the client without passing through the user-agent, where it could be exposed; the grant is optimized for confidential clients.

The implicit grant, for in-browser JavaScript clients, issues an access token directly with no intermediate code and saves round trips, but does not authenticate the client, exposes the token to the user-agent, and issues no refresh token.

The resource owner password credentials grant exchanges the user's own username and password for a token; use it only where the client is highly trusted, such as the device operating system, and no other grant is available.
That grant carries higher risk because it keeps the password anti-pattern the protocol avoids: the client could abuse or leak the password, so servers and clients should minimize its use.

In the client credentials grant the client authenticates with only its own credentials, when acting on its own behalf or on access previously arranged; only confidential clients may use it, and a refresh token should not be included.
Extension grants use an absolute URI, defined by the authorization server, as the grant_type value at the token endpoint, with any extra parameters needed.

title: Authorization code grant
article: rfc>6749#4. Obtaining Authorization > 4.1. Authorization Code Grant

definition.text: The authorization code grant is a redirection-based flow that obtains access and refresh tokens via the user-agent and is optimized for confidential clients.

facts.text: The client directs the user-agent to the authorization endpoint with its client identifier, requested scope, local state and a redirection URI; the server authenticates the resource owner and establishes whether they grant or deny access.
If access is granted, the server redirects the user-agent to the redirection URI with an authorization code and any state the client provided.

The client then requests a token from the token endpoint, authenticating and repeating the redirection URI; the server authenticates it, validates the code, checks the URI matches, and returns an access token and optionally a refresh token.
The state parameter is recommended and should be used to prevent cross-site request forgery; the server returns it unchanged.
The code must expire shortly after it is issued, with a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes recommended, and the client must not use it more than once.
If a code is used more than once, the server must deny the request and should revoke tokens previously issued from it; the code is bound to the client identifier and redirection URI.
The token request is a POST to the token endpoint with grant_type authorization_code; confidential clients, or any client issued credentials, must authenticate there.
If the redirection URI is missing, invalid or mismatching, the server should inform the resource owner and must not automatically redirect the user-agent to it.

definition.text: An access token is a credential, usually an opaque string, representing an authorization issued to the client for accessing protected resources.

facts.text: Tokens represent specific scopes and durations of access, granted by the resource owner and enforced by the resource server and authorization server.
A token may be an identifier used to retrieve the authorization information, or may self-contain that information in a verifiable manner, as a string of data plus a signature.

It replaces constructs such as username and password with a single token the resource server understands, allowing tokens more restrictive than the grant that produced them and sparing the resource server many authentication methods.
The client should request the minimal scope necessary; the server may issue a token with less rights than requested and must tell the client the scope actually granted.

The client reaches protected resources by presenting the token to the resource server; the authorization server must ensure tokens cannot be forged or guessed, keeping the guessing probability at or below 2^(-128).
Tokens must be kept confidential in transit and storage, shared only among the authorization server, the resource servers they are valid for and the client, and sent only over TLS.

definition.text: A refresh token is a credential the authorization server issues to the client for obtaining new access tokens.

facts.text: It lets the client get a new access token when the current one expires or becomes invalid, or extra tokens with identical or narrower scope, so access tokens can be short-lived with fewer permissions than the owner authorized.
Issuing a refresh token is optional at the authorization server's discretion, and it is included when the access token is issued.
Unlike access tokens, refresh tokens are intended only for authorization servers and are never sent to resource servers.

When the access token expires, the client authenticates with the authorization server and presents the refresh token; the server validates it and issues a new access token and, optionally, a new refresh token.
The requested scope must not include any scope not originally granted, a refresh token is bound to the client it was issued to, and if a new one is issued the client must discard the old one.

Refresh tokens must be kept confidential and sent only over TLS; rotation, issuing a new one with each refresh and invalidating the old, reveals theft because attacker or legitimate client will present an invalidated token.

Before the protocol starts the client registers with the authorization server, giving its client type and redirection URIs; the server issues a unique client identifier, which is not a secret and must not alone authenticate the client.
A confidential client can keep its credentials secret, for example on a secure server; a public client cannot, for example an installed native application or a browser-based application.

In the profiles, a web application is confidential and keeps tokens on its server, a user-agent-based application is public, and a native application is public with any embedded credentials assumed extractable.

The authorization endpoint obtains authorization via user-agent redirection, the token endpoint exchanges a grant for an access token, and the client's redirection endpoint receives responses; confidential clients must authenticate at the token endpoint.

definition.text: Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is an OAuth 2.0 extension that stops an attacker who intercepts an authorization code from redeeming it, by binding the code to a one-time secret only the real client holds.

facts.text: OAuth 2.0 public clients are open to an authorization code interception attack: the attacker captures the code on a path not protected by TLS, such as inter-application communication in the client's operating system, and trades it for an access token.

On a phone, a malicious app can register as a handler for the legitimate app's custom URI scheme and receive the code; secrets provisioned in a client binary cannot be considered confidential, so a client secret does not stop it.

For each authorization request the client creates a random secret, the code verifier, derives a code challenge from it, and sends the challenge with the request; the authorization endpoint responds as usual but records the challenge and its transformation method.

The client later sends the authorization code together with the code verifier in the access token request; the server transforms the verifier, compares it with the stored challenge, and denies access if they differ, returning an invalid_grant error.
An attacker who intercepts the authorization code cannot redeem it, because the verifier is a one-time key that was never sent over any channel the attacker can observe.

The code verifier is a high-entropy cryptographic random string of 43 to 128 unreserved characters; the client should give it at least 256 bits of entropy, for example a 32-octet random sequence base64url-encoded into 43 characters.

Two transformations exist: plain, where the challenge equals the verifier, and S256, the base64url encoding of the SHA-256 hash of the verifier. A client that can use S256 must use it, because every PKCE server must support S256.

Plain should not be used in new implementations, because its challenge is the verifier and an eavesdropper can see it; a client must never downgrade to plain after trying S256. No salt is needed for S256.

sources.title: RFC 7636: Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients

definition.text: The claims of a JWT are the name/value members of the JSON object, called the JWT Claims Set, that the token conveys.

facts.text: Claim names fall into three classes. Registered names are listed in the IANA registry, public names must be registered or collision-resistant, and private names are agreed between producer and consumer and can collide, so they need caution.

The registered claims are a starting point, not a mandatory set: each application defines which it uses and when they are required. Their names are short because a core goal of JWTs is a compact representation.

The iss claim names the principal that issued the token, sub names its subject, which must be unique within the issuer or globally, and iat records when it was issued, so the token's age can be determined.

The aud claim lists the intended recipients: each principal that processes the token must identify itself with a value in it, and if the claim is present and the processor is not named, the JWT must be rejected.
A token must not be accepted on or after its exp time, nor before its nbf time; implementers may allow a small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew.
The jti claim gives the token a unique identifier, assigned so that a collision is negligibly probable even across several issuers, and it can be used to prevent the token from being replayed.

Claim names within a token must be unique, so a parser must reject duplicates or keep only the last one; claims an implementation does not understand must be ignored unless the application requires otherwise.

title: Creating and validating a JWT
article: rfc>7519#7. Creating and Validating JWTs > 7.2. Validating a JWT

definition.text: Creating a JWT builds a claims set and then signs or encrypts it, and validating one reverses those steps and rejects the token if any step fails.

facts.text: To create a JWT, build the Claims Set, take its UTF-8 octets as the message, and build a JOSE header; then sign the message as a JWS payload or encrypt it as JWE plaintext. No canonicalization is needed.
For nested signing or encryption, the resulting JWS or JWE becomes the new message, and the steps repeat with a cty header value of JWT; otherwise that JWS or JWE is the finished JWT.

Validation first checks that the JWT contains at least one period. The part before the first period is base64url-decoded into a JOSE header that must be valid JSON and contain only parameters the implementation understands and supports.
It then decides whether the JWT is a JWS or a JWE and validates the signature or decrypts accordingly; the message is the decoded JWS payload or the decrypted plaintext.

If the header's cty value is JWT, the message is itself a nested JWT and validation starts again on it; otherwise the message is base64url-decoded and must be valid JSON, which becomes the Claims Set.

If any step fails the JWT must be rejected as invalid input. Even a JWT that validates should be rejected unless its algorithms are acceptable, because which algorithms may be used is an application decision.

definition.text: A JWT is carried either as a signed JWS or an encrypted JWE, may nest one inside the other, and can also be left unsecured.

facts.text: The JOSE header describes the cryptographic operations applied to the claims: in a JWS they are digitally signed or MACed and form the JWS payload, in a JWE they are the plaintext that is encrypted.

A JWT may be enclosed in another JWE or JWS to create a Nested JWT. When both are needed, producers should normally sign first and then encrypt, which prevents stripping the signature and gives the signer privacy.
An Unsecured JWT is a JWS with the alg value none and an empty signature, allowed for cases where the content is secured by some means other than a signature or encryption inside the JWT.
A conforming implementation must support only HS256 and none; RS256 and ES256 are recommended, and support for other algorithms, encrypted JWTs and Nested JWTs is optional.
